name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,369

entries.clue: Party cheers rabid, vacuous old fool (6)

indicatorNotes.vacuous: A vacuous thing is empty in the middle, so the word beside it keeps only the letters at its two edges.

blocks.note: a do is a party — the office do, a birthday do
ta is the British thank-you, and cheers does the same job
emptied out, rabid keeps its first and last letters only

annotation.surface: A party raises a cheer for someone raving and empty-headed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Party' looks political in a sentence about slogans and cheering, and is the social kind. The definition points at dotage, the feeble-mindedness that comes with great age.
annotation.definitionFit: A dotard is someone whose wits have gone with age, so old fool names both halves of it at once.

entries.clue: Spotted orchard’s last fruit (6)

annotation.definitionNote: Dapple is an adjective as well as a verb — a dapple-grey horse — so 'spotted' is describing markings here, not reporting that somebody noticed something.

indicatorNotes.last: The last of a word is the letter it ends on, and that single letter is all that is taken.

blocks.note: the letter orchard finishes on
the fruit an orchard is likeliest to be growing

annotation.surface: Someone points out the last fruit still hanging in the orchard.
annotation.walkthrough: Reading 'spotted' as the past tense of noticing is the trap; it is an adjective about markings. The rest runs on as one unbroken phrase, so nothing shows where the definition stops.
annotation.definitionFit: A dapple coat is one covered in patches of contrasting colour, which is what a spotted animal or surface looks like.

entries.clue: Unthinkingly state anti-Communist slogan? (4,3)

blocks.note: to produce the same tired line yet again, as a spokesman does
a Trot is a Trotskyist, so shouted as two words this tells one to clear off

annotation.surface: A slogan being chanted at a demonstration without much thought behind it.
annotation.walkthrough: Trot is British shorthand for a Trotskyist, the far-left faction Labour spent the 1980s expelling. The question mark marks the second reading as a joke rather than a dictionary sense.
annotation.definitionFit: To trot out a phrase is to produce it by reflex; split between the two words instead, it becomes an order shouted at a Trot.

entries.clue: Separation initially reported in paper (4)

indicatorNotes.initially: Initially asks how words begin, so only the opening letter of each one beside it is used.

blocks.note: the first letters of the two words
the FT is the Financial Times, the pink British business daily

annotation.surface: A split between people getting its first mention in the newspaper.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reported' wants to be a signal that something is heard rather than spelt, and it is only handing over a letter. The pink paper is a stock crossword newspaper.
annotation.definitionFit: A rift is the gap that opens between two people who have fallen out, which is the separation the word names.

entries.clue: Frozen topping that is better for keeping cold (3,3)

indicatorNotes.keeping: Keeping a thing means holding on to it, so the letter named goes inside the word that does the keeping.

blocks.note: ie, short for the Latin id est
c is the standard abbreviation for cold, as marked on a tap
to cap a rival's offer is to better it

annotation.surface: A dessert topping that improves for being kept chilled.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Better' has to be heard as a verb before anything moves. The definition is polar rather than culinary, which is why 'topping' reads as pudding for as long as it can.
annotation.definitionFit: An ice cap is the permanent sheet of ice lying over a polar region — frozen, and sitting on top of what it covers.

entries.clue: Wins children’s game, we hear (8)

indicatorNotes.we hear: What we hear is the sound of a word rather than its spelling, so the letters only have to match aloud.

blocks.note: conkers is the British playground game of swinging a horse chestnut on a string at an opponent's

annotation.surface: Someone keeps winning the children's game, going by what people say.
annotation.walkthrough: Conkers are horse chestnuts, threaded on shoelaces and smashed together in British school playgrounds every autumn. The plural s survives the crossing from sound to spelling untouched.
annotation.definitionFit: To conquer an opponent is to beat them outright, so wins covers it, and both verbs take the same third-person -s.

entries.clue: Yearn for Sven, naked in bed (5)

indicatorNotes.naked: Something naked has had its covering stripped off, so the word loses the letter at each end.
indicatorNotes.in: In puts one thing inside another, so what comes before it is buried in the word that follows.

blocks.note: a cot is a bed
stripped of the letters at each end, Sven leaves the middle pair

annotation.surface: Sven lies undressed in bed, wanted badly by somebody.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma after 'Sven' hides that 'naked' is an instruction and not a description of him. A cot is the setter's standard three-letter bed.
annotation.definitionFit: To covet is to want badly something that is somebody else's, which is what yearning for a thing means; both verbs take an object.

entries.clue: Miserable mate on crack (6)

indicatorNotes.on: In a down entry one thing sits on top of another, so the mate is written above the crack.

blocks.note: a pal is a mate
to have a crack at something is to have a try at it

annotation.surface: A wretched friend in a bad way on crack.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crack' points at the drug in the surface and is the everyday 'have a crack at it'. Down clues let 'on' mean directly above, which is what fixes the order.
annotation.definitionFit: A paltry sum is a miserably small one, and the two adjectives sit in front of the same nouns — paltry wages, miserable wages.

entries.clue: Present academic referee retiring (7)

indicatorNotes.retiring: To retire is to go back the way you came, so the word beside it is written out in reverse.

blocks.note: a prof is an academic
a referee is a ref, turned back to front

annotation.surface: A retiring referee is handed a present by the academic.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Retiring' reads as the referee's final season and is a turn-round instruction. 'Present' is the verb for holding something out, not the parcel the surface pictures.
annotation.definitionFit: To proffer something is to hold it out for another to take, which is exactly what present means as a verb.

entries.clue: Report of turbulent short life (5,4)

indicatorNotes.turbulent: Turbulence throws whatever it touches about, so the letters beside it will not stay in the order given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: An account of a stormy life cut short.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Report of' at the front looks like an instruction to listen for a sound-alike, and is the definition with a link word. The letter count against the enumeration settles it.
annotation.definitionFit: The bang a gun makes is called its report, and a rifle shot is heard as precisely that single sharp crack.

entries.clue: Reviewed extract from incredible Vonnegut book (5)

indicatorNotes.Reviewed: Re-viewed is looked at a second time from the other end, so the run of letters is read backwards.
indicatorNotes.extract from: Extracting takes a run of letters already sitting in the words, in the order they stand.

blocks.note: the letters bridging 'incredibLE VONnegut', read back to front

annotation.surface: A reviewer quotes a passage out of an astonishing Vonnegut book.
annotation.walkthrough: Vonnegut wrote books, so the surface points where the definition does and the buried run is easy to walk past. Hidden answers that span a gap between words are the hardest sort to see.
annotation.definitionFit: A novel is a book-length work of fiction, so 'book' defines it by kind rather than by synonym.

entries.clue: Can finally collect money (4)

indicatorNotes.finally: Finally points at the end of a word, so its closing letter is the only one used.

blocks.note: can is the American word for the lavatory, which in Britain is the loo
the letter collect ends on

annotation.surface: Somebody gets round to collecting the money at last.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Can' is doing plumbing duty rather than meaning a tin or permission. A one-word definition at the end of a short clue gives very little to aim at.
annotation.definitionFit: Loot is money carried off — from a raid, a till or a party bag — so it sits squarely inside the everyday sense of money.

entries.clue: Nervous bet after tip from accountant (8)

indicatorNotes.after: What comes after a thing is written second, so the bet lands behind the letter taken.
indicatorNotes.tip from: The tip of a word is its very front, so the letter it starts with is what comes away.

blocks.note: the opening letter of accountant
British for a small casual bet, the few pounds put on a horse

annotation.surface: An accountant's tip leads to a jittery wager.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tip' in a sentence about accountants and betting reads as inside information, and is a letter-picking instruction. A flutter is the modest sort of bet placed at a high-street bookmaker's.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone all aflutter is fidgety and agitated, so nervous covers it — both are adjectives for the same state.

entries.clue: Old man turned on generator, as observed (8)

annotation.definitionNote: 'As observed' gives the way a thing strikes the eye rather than a one-word synonym; what is apparent is what observation shows, as opposed to what has to be worked out.

indicatorNotes.turned: Something turned faces the other way, so the letters beside it are read in reverse.
indicatorNotes.on: In a down entry one part sits on another, so the old man goes above the generator.

blocks.note: an old man is a pa, climbing this column
whoever generates the children is their parent

annotation.surface: The old man was seen starting the generator up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turned on' reads as one phrase about switching a machine on and is two separate instructions. A generator in the wordplay is a person, not a machine.
annotation.definitionFit: What is apparent is what shows plainly on looking, so it answers to a thing taken as observed rather than inferred.

entries.clue: Erect post, disguised and completely hidden from the public (3,6)

indicatorNotes.disguised: A disguise changes how a thing looks without changing what it is, so the same letters appear in another arrangement.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Putting up a post in disguise, where nobody can see it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Erect' looks like an instruction to stand something upright, which would turn a down answer round and can do nothing in an across one. Both words are fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Top secret is the highest security classification a government gives, so what carries it is kept wholly out of public sight.

entries.clue: Leaders of the Resistance are irate, talking of recent renegade (7)

indicatorNotes.Leaders of: The leader of a word is the letter at its head, so each word in the run gives up only its first.

blocks.clueFragment: the Resistance are irate, talking of recent
blocks.note: the initial letters of those seven words, in order

annotation.surface: Angry Resistance leaders discussing somebody who has just changed sides.
annotation.walkthrough: Seven initials in a row is a long run to trust, and 'Leaders of the Resistance' reads as people rather than as an instruction. The definition is the single word at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: A traitor deserts their own side and betrays it, which is what renegade names — both nouns for the same person.

entries.clue: Son makes fun of baggy clothing (6)

annotation.definitionNote: Clothing is a mass noun and the answer a plural, a swap crosswords allow because both name garments taken in bulk rather than one item.

blocks.note: s is the standard abbreviation for son, as used on a family tree
to mock somebody is to make fun of them

annotation.surface: A son teasing somebody about their loose clothes.
annotation.walkthrough: No word in the clue announces itself as an instruction, which is the mark of a plain charade. 'Makes fun of' has to be heard as a third-person verb before the letter in front of it has anywhere to go.
annotation.definitionFit: A smock is the loose overshirt worn by painters and farm workers, cut wide on purpose, which is baggy clothing.

entries.clue: Cautioned Washington editor about sailors (6)

indicatorNotes.about: Something set about a thing is wrapped round it, so the letters named last end up in the middle.

blocks.note: WA is the postal abbreviation for Washington state
the RN is the Royal Navy, Britain's sailors
ed is the standard short form of editor

annotation.surface: A Washington newspaper editor being told something about sailors.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as 'on the subject of' in a sentence full of journalism and is a wrapping instruction. Washington is the state, not the capital city.
annotation.definitionFit: To warn somebody is to tell them of trouble coming, which is what cautioned reports — both past tenses of the same act.

entries.clue: Shunning publicity, my head is spinning (5,3)

indicatorNotes.spinning: A spin sends a thing round and round, so the letters beside it come to rest in a different order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Somebody avoiding the press complains of dizziness.
annotation.walkthrough: 'My head is spinning' is a complete idiom, which hides that all three of those words are fodder. 'Head' usually asks for a first letter, and here it does not.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody media shy keeps clear of interviews and cameras, which is shunning publicity.

entries.clue: Grave inspiring Gray’s first elegy (5)

indicatorNotes.inspiring: To inspire is to breathe in, so the word draws the letter beside it inside itself.
indicatorNotes.first: First asks for the letter a word starts with and nothing more.

blocks.note: a grave situation is a dire one
the letter Gray starts with

annotation.surface: A grave in a churchyard that moved Gray to write his first elegy.
annotation.walkthrough: Thomas Gray wrote 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard', so graves, Gray and elegies belong together and no word stands out as wordplay. 'Grave' is the adjective meaning serious.
annotation.definitionFit: A dirge is the slow lament sung over the dead, and an elegy is that same mourning for the dead set down in verse.

entries.clue: Story is great fun when read backwards (4)

indicatorNotes.when read backwards: Reading backwards starts at the last letter and works towards the first.

blocks.note: something that is great fun is a gas, and that comes back the other way

annotation.surface: A tale that turns out to be hilarious if you start from the end.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A gas' is slang for something hugely enjoyable, and the clue leaves you to supply the article yourself. Nothing else in the sentence contributes a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A saga is a long tale of events told through from beginning to end, so story is a plain synonym.

entries.clue: Nasty cases of unnerving lurgy (4)

indicatorNotes.cases of: A case is what encloses a thing, so each word gives up just the letters at its two ends.

blocks.note: the outside letters of unnerving
the outside letters of lurgy — the lurgy is British slang for whatever unnamed illness is going round

annotation.surface: A nasty run of cases of some unsettling bug.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cases of' fits a sentence about illness so neatly that it stops looking like an instruction. The lurgy is the joke name Britons give whatever they have caught.
annotation.definitionFit: Ugly means repellent to look at, and an ugly mood or an ugly scene is a nasty one — the same adjective either way.

entries.clue: Scoundrels start to expostulate and swear (5)

indicatorNotes.start to: The start of a word is its opening letter, and only that one comes away.

blocks.note: a cur is a mongrel dog, and so a contemptible man
the opening letter of expostulate

annotation.surface: Scoundrels begin to protest loudly and turn the air blue.
annotation.walkthrough: Both ends of the clue suit the picture of a row, so the definition hides in plain sight at the back. Curs are dogs before they are people, which is where the insult gets its bite.
annotation.definitionFit: To curse is to come out with an oath, which is swear in its bad-language sense rather than its taking-an-oath one.

entries.clue: Strengthen thing that teen regularly dropped (7)

indicatorNotes.regularly dropped: Letting letters go at regular intervals means losing every second one, and what stays is read in the order it stood.

blocks.note: the first letter of the run and every other one after it through 'thingthatteen'

annotation.surface: A thing the teenager keeps dropping needs making firmer.
annotation.walkthrough: Alternate-letter runs usually hide inside one or two words; this one stretches across three, so counting is the only way in. The run has to start on the very first letter to come out right.
annotation.definitionFit: To tighten a bolt, a rule or a defence is to make it firmer and harder to shift, which is strengthening it.

entries.clue: Hustle involved detective (6)

indicatorNotes.involved: Something involved is tangled up, so the letters beside it are knotted into a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A detective caught up in somebody's con trick.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hustle' is a con trick in the surface and a bag of six letters in the wordplay, and 'involved' means tangled rather than mixed up in a crime. Two words is the shortest a clue of this kind gets.
annotation.definitionFit: A sleuth is a detective, the word coming from the sleuth-hound that followed a trail by scent.

entries.clue: Cross section of Clichy Bridge (6)

indicatorNotes.section of: A section is a piece cut out of something longer, so a run of letters is taken just as it stands.

blocks.note: the run bridging the gap in 'clicHY BRIDge'

annotation.surface: A cross-section drawing of the bridge at Clichy.
annotation.walkthrough: Clichy is a suburb on the northern edge of Paris, which is all the proper noun is there for. 'Cross' is the breeder's noun, not the adjective for annoyed.
annotation.definitionFit: A hybrid is the offspring of two different varieties, which gardeners and dog breeders call a cross.
